title: t01 Overfitting
tagline: Overfitting is memorizing the misprints and mistaking them for real patterns.

items.title: A model's near-perfect
items.subtitle: A model's near-perfect on the data it learned from, then fails on new data.

items.title: Usually that's not a bug in the code.
items.subtitle: Usually that's not a bug in the code. It's a problem called overfitting.

items.title: Overfitting is when a model learns
items.subtitle: Overfitting is when a model learns its practice data too literally, flukes and all, so it does worse on new data.

items.title: Picture a student who memorizes
items.subtitle: Picture a student who memorizes every answer in the workbook, misprints included, and scores 100 every time.

items.title: But on the exam
items.subtitle: But on the exam, the questions change just a little, and he's lost.

items.title: The workbook is the model's data
items.subtitle: The workbook is the model's data, and the misprints are what we call noise.

items.title: When a model memorizes the noise
items.subtitle: When a model memorizes the noise as if it were a real pattern, that's overfitting.

items.title: Let's see it happen.
items.subtitle: Let's see it happen. These 10 points are our training data, our practice questions.

items.title: They roughly follow a pattern
items.subtitle: They roughly follow a pattern, but each one is nudged off by a bit of random wobble. That wobble is the noise.

items.title: The model's job is to find
items.subtitle: The model's job is to find that pattern and predict new points.

items.title: The first model is too simple.
items.subtitle: The first model is too simple. It can only draw a straight line.

items.title: The farther a point is from the line
items.subtitle: The farther a point is from the line, the bigger the mistake. The average mistake is the error.

items.title: The line can't even get
items.subtitle: The line can't even get the practice questions right. That's called underfitting.

items.title: The second model is a gentle curve.
items.subtitle: The second model is a gentle curve. It misses some points, but it catches the overall trend.

items.title: The third is really complicated
items.subtitle: The third is really complicated, twisting and turning through every single point, so its practice error is zero.

items.title: So which one do you think
items.subtitle: So which one do you think will do best on new questions?

items.title: Now we test them on 6
items.subtitle: Now we test them on 6 points they've never seen. That's the test data, our exam.

items.title: The second model stays
items.subtitle: The second model stays close to all of them, so it does best.

items.title: The third zigzags between the practice
items.subtitle: The third zigzags between the practice points and misses some new points by a lot.

items.title: Its exam error is more than twenty
items.subtitle: Its exam error is more than twenty times the second model's.

items.title: That's because it memorized the noise
items.subtitle: That's because it memorized the noise, and noise is random, so it doesn't repeat on new questions. That's overfitting.

items.title: Underfitting is easy to spot:
items.subtitle: Underfitting is easy to spot: it does badly on practice and exam questions.

items.title: Overfitting is sneakier
items.subtitle: Overfitting is sneakier, because its practice score can look amazing. Here, its practice error was zero.

items.title: Here's another way to see it:
items.subtitle: Here's another way to see it: think of learning as compression.

items.title: To remember these 10 points exactly
items.subtitle: To remember these 10 points exactly, you'd need to store 10 numbers, one height per point.

items.title: The second curve takes just 4 numbers
items.subtitle: The second curve takes just 4 numbers, yet stays close to the points and predicts new ones well. That's compression.

items.title: The third curve needs 10
items.subtitle: The third curve needs 10 numbers to go through 10 points.

items.title: Ten numbers for ten points
items.subtitle: Ten numbers for ten points is no compression at all, so the noise got saved too.

items.title: Good compression keeps the pattern
items.subtitle: Good compression keeps the pattern and throws out the noise. Squeeze too hard, like that straight line, and you lose the pattern too.

items.title: Take Google Flu Trends.
items.subtitle: Take Google Flu Trends. Google once used people's searches to estimate what share of doctor visits involved flu-like symptoms.

items.title: At first, it sifted 50 million search terms
items.subtitle: At first, it sifted 50 million search terms to match about 1,100 flu data points.

items.title: With far more terms than data points
items.subtitle: With far more terms than data points, it was bound to pick up some that just happened to spike in winter.

items.title: Researchers said this was overfitting.
items.subtitle: Researchers said this was overfitting. It was part flu detector, part winter detector.

items.title: Later versions missed too.
items.subtitle: Later versions missed too. In 100 out of 108 weeks, they guessed too high.

items.title: How do you spot overfitting and stop it?
items.subtitle: How do you spot overfitting and stop it? Here are three common ways.

items.title: First, set aside some data as a mock exam
items.subtitle: First, set aside some data as a mock exam, called a validation set.

items.title: Use it to pick your model
items.subtitle: Use it to pick your model and catch overfitting early. Save the real exam for the very end.

items.title: To be honest
items.subtitle: To be honest, in our experiment we picked the model by its exam score. On a real project, you shouldn't.

items.title: Second, collect more data
items.subtitle: Second, collect more data, and more varied data, so noise and coincidences are less likely to pass for patterns.

items.title: Third, give the model a rule:
items.subtitle: Third, give the model a rule: overly complicated curves get penalized, so it won't chase the noise. That's called regularization.

items.title: Overfitting is memorizing the misprints
items.subtitle: Overfitting is memorizing the misprints and mistaking them for real patterns.

items.title: So whenever you feel like
items.subtitle: So whenever you feel like you totally get something, try a question you've never seen.
